nameStory: This little plant gets its name from its prostrate (lying flat) growth habit and its love of sandy, disturbed soils - hence 'sandmat.' Like a tiny green carpet, it spreads flat against the ground, forming mats that hug sandy roadsides and pathways. The name perfectly captures how it lives: low, sprawling, and right at home in gritty places.
description: Prostrate sandmat is a tiny, creeping annual weed that forms flat mats along the ground. This diminutive member of the spurge family rarely grows taller than your thumb, instead spreading outward in thin, branching stems that radiate from a central point. Its small, oval leaves and inconspicuous flowers make it easy to overlook, but once you spot one mat, you'll often find many more nearby. Like other spurges, it produces a milky white sap when broken.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms perfectly flat mats that press tight against the ground, with thin reddish stems radiating outward from the center like spokes of a wheel

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny oval leaves, smaller than your pinky nail, arranged opposite each other along the stems with smooth edges and a slightly waxy feel

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Extremely small, inconspicuous flowers tucked into leaf joints - you'll need to look closely to spot these tiny greenish clusters

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thin, often reddish stems that feel slightly succulent and release milky white sap when pinched or broken

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Microscopic three-chambered capsules that split open explosively when ripe, shooting seeds away from the parent plant

habitat: Look for prostrate sandmat in disturbed, sandy areas like roadsides, parking lot edges, and sidewalk cracks throughout New England. It thrives in compacted, nutrient-poor soils where few other plants can compete. You'll often find it growing alongside other weedy species in urban and suburban environments.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate as soil warms, with tiny seedlings beginning to form their characteristic radiating pattern of growth.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and flower throughout the warm months, forming obvious flat mats in sandy, disturbed areas.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules mature and explosively disperse, while plants begin to turn reddish-brown before dying with the first frost.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants are completely gone, leaving only seeds in the soil to sprout the following spring.

funFact: When mature seed pods are touched or disturbed, they explode like tiny cannons, shooting seeds up to several feet away with an audible 'pop' - it's nature's own miniature artillery system!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with spotted spurge, but prostrate sandmat forms much flatter, more perfectly circular mats and lacks the dark red spots on the leaves that give spotted spurge its name. Remember: truly prostrate = prostrate sandmat.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the same family as the Christmas poinsettia, this humble weed couldn't look more different from its showy relative. The milky sap that all spurges share can be mildly irritating to skin and eyes, so avoid rubbing your face after handling these plants.
compareHints: Among New England's spurges, prostrate sandmat is uniquely flat-growing - most other spurges like cypress spurge or flowering spurge grow upright. Seaside sandmat is similarly prostrate but has much thicker, more succulent leaves and grows only in coastal sand dunes, while prostrate sandmat prefers disturbed inland soils.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other spurges in New England that typically have broader, more conventional leaves, cypress spurge is instantly recognizable by its needle-like foliage.
Among New England's spurges, spotted spurge is unique for its ground-hugging mat formation and distinctly spotted leaves.
Among New England's spurges, seaside sandmat is unique in its completely prostrate, mat-forming habit and coastal habitat.
Among New England spurges, slender leafy spurge is distinguished by its tall, narrow growth form and lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's spurges, nodding spurge is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth and drooping flower clusters.
Unlike other New England spurges which are mostly weedy annuals with thin leaves, Donkey Tail is a perennial succulent with thick, fleshy foliage.
Among New England's sandmat spurges, Wormseed Sandmat is distinguished by its perfectly circular growth pattern and distinctively ridged seeds.
Among New England spurges, caper spurge is unique for its large size and architectural growth habit - most other spurges are low-growing weeds or small garden plants.
Unlike the tall, weedy leafy spurge or the ground-hugging spotted spurge, cushion spurge maintains a perfectly rounded, compact form.
Among New England spurges, petty spurge is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
Flowering spurge towers over most of its spurge relatives in New England, which tend to be low, mat-forming plants like spotted spurge or cypress spurge.
Snow-on-the-mountain is easily distinguished from other New England spurges by its distinctive white-margined leaves - most other spurges in our region have plain green foliage.

Leafy spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its tall, upright growth and dense leafy appearance - most of its relatives like spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat are low, sprawling plants.
Among New England spurges, graceful spurge stands out for its relatively tall, upright growth compared to the ground-hugging spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat.
Among New England's spurges, thymeleaf sandmat is distinguished by its ground-hugging mat formation and tiny thyme-like leaves.
Sweet spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its clumping perennial growth habit and relatively large, oval leaves.
Among New England spurges, green poinsettia stands out for its distinctly hairy, toothed leaves - most other spurges have smooth or nearly smooth leaves.
Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the spotted stems of spotted spurge, David's spurge has broader, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs.
Unlike other New England spurges that have broader, more typical-looking leaves, grassleaf spurge's ultra-narrow foliage makes it unique in the region.
Unlike cypress spurge with its needle-like leaves or spotted spurge that grows as a low mat, eggleaf spurge stands upright with distinctly oval, toothed leaves.
Compared to other New England spurges, Florida hammock sandmat is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and extremely low, tight mat-forming habit.
Matted sandmat is flatter and more perfectly mat-forming than most other spurges in our region.
Among New England's spurges, ribseed sandmat is distinguished by its extremely rare occurrence and the ribbed seeds that give it its name.
